items.prompt: Which article is the feminine singular definite article in the nominative case?

options.label: den
die
das
der

rubric: `die` is the feminine singular nominative article.
`der` is masculine and `das` is neuter; `den` is masculine accusative.

items.prompt: What does the German word `Entschuldigung` mean?

options.label: Thank you very much
Excuse me / sorry
Good night to you
You are welcome

rubric: `Entschuldigung` is used to apologise or get someone's attention.
Distractors are other common polite phrases that learners mix up.

items.prompt: Which form completes the sentence: `Ich ___ müde.` (sein)

options.label: sind
ist
bist
bin

rubric: `ich` takes `bin`.
`bist` goes with `du`, `ist` with er/sie/es, `sind` with wir/sie.

items.prompt: In a normal German statement (main clause), where does the conjugated verb stand?

options.label: In the final position
In the second position
In the third position
In the first position

rubric: The verb-second rule applies to main clauses.
Verb-final is a feature of subordinate clauses, which learners wrongly generalise.

items.prompt: How is the German letter `ß` pronounced?

options.label: Like the sch in schon
Like a sharp s sound
Like an English b, from its shape
Like the ts in Zeit sound

rubric: `ß` (Eszett) represents a voiceless s sound, like ss.
Its shape makes learners confuse it with b.

items.prompt: Which of these are definite articles in the nominative case? Select all that apply.

options.label: den
der
das
die
dem

rubric: `der`, `die` and `das` are the nominative definite articles.
`dem` is dative and `den` is accusative (masculine) or dative plural.

items.prompt: You walk into a bakery at 8 a.m. in Germany and want to greet the person at the counter politely. Which phrase do you use?

options.label: Gute Nacht
Guten Abend
Guten Morgen
Auf Wiedersehen

rubric: `Guten Morgen` is the morning greeting.
`Gute Nacht` and `Auf Wiedersehen` are for parting, and `Guten Abend` is for evening.

items.prompt: Which sentence follows German capitalization rules?

options.label: ich sehe einen hund im garten.
Ich Sehe Einen Hund Im Garten.
Ich sehe einen Hund im Garten.
Ich sehe einen hund im Garten.

rubric: All German nouns are capitalized, while other words are only capitalized at the start of a sentence.
Distractors skip noun capitalization or capitalize every word.

items.prompt: Why is it `Ich fahre mit dem Bus` and not `mit den Bus`?

options.label: The preposition mit always takes the dative case
Bus is the object of fahren, so it takes the accusative
Bus is plural here, so it takes den in the dative
Verbs of motion like fahren always need the dative

rubric: `mit` is a dative preposition, and masculine dative is `dem`.
Distractors blame number, subject role or the verb rather than the preposition.

items.prompt: Which sentence has correct word order when it starts with `Heute`?

options.label: Heute ich ins Kino gehe.
Heute gehe ich ins Kino.
Heute gehe ins Kino ich.
Heute ich gehe ins Kino.

rubric: The verb stays second, so the subject moves after it (inversion).
`Heute ich gehe` keeps English order and ignores verb-second.

items.prompt: In the question `Wie heißen Sie?`, what does the capitalized `Sie` mean?

options.label: You, in the formal register
It, referring to a feminine object
They, referring to a group of people
She, referring to a woman nearby

rubric: Capital `Sie` with a plural verb form is the formal you.
Learners confuse it with she or they because the words look identical.

items.prompt: The noun `Mädchen` (girl) takes `das`. What explains its grammatical gender?

options.label: It is an exception with no pattern
The ending -chen makes nouns neuter
All nouns for young people are neuter
Girls are female, so it should be `die`

rubric: The diminutive suffix -chen always gives a neuter noun.
Natural sex does not decide German gender, and the suffix rule is a pattern, not an exception.

items.prompt: Which of these are correct present-tense forms of `machen`? Select all that apply.

options.label: ich mache
wir macht
er macht
ihr machen
du machst

rubric: Regular endings: -e, -st, -t for ich, du, er.
`wir` takes -en and `ihr` takes -t, so the last two are swapped.

items.prompt: A learner writes `Ich habe ein Hund.` Her teacher corrects it to `Ich habe einen Hund.` The learner asks why the article changed.

options.label: Hund is plural here, so the article takes an -en ending
Hund is a feminine noun, so the article needs an -en ending
Hund is the direct object, so masculine ein becomes einen
After haben the article always adds -en, whatever the noun's gender

rubric: Direct objects take the accusative, where masculine `ein` becomes `einen`.
Distractors misread number, gender or the verb's role.

items.prompt: In the sentence `Morgen gehe ich ins Kino.` the verb comes before `ich`. Why?

options.label: The conjugated verb must stand in second position in a main clause
The verb moves forward because `ich` is in the dative case here
German puts the subject after any word that names a time of day
Sentences with a direction like `ins Kino` always put the verb first

rubric: German main clauses keep the conjugated verb in second position, so the subject moves behind the time word.
Distractors invent special rules about time words, case or prepositions.

items.prompt: In `Ich sehe den Hund.` what does the article `den` tell you?

options.label: Hund is a plural dative noun, as after mit or von
Hund is a neuter noun marking who owns something
Hund is the subject, the one who does the seeing
Hund is a masculine direct object (accusative)

rubric: `den` is the masculine accusative article, marking the direct object.
Distractors confuse it with the subject, dative plural or genitive.

items.prompt: Which of these prepositions always takes the dative case?

options.label: ohne
mit
durch
für

rubric: `mit` always takes the dative.
The others (durch, für, ohne) always take the accusative.

items.prompt: How is the letter `w` in `Wasser` pronounced?

options.label: Like English `w` in water
Like English `f` in fast
Like English `y` in yes
Like English `v` in very

rubric: German `w` sounds like English `v`.
Learners often carry over the English `w` sound.

items.prompt: Why is `Ich habe kein Auto.` correct, while `Ich habe nicht Auto.` is not?

options.label: `kein` negates a noun that would take `ein` or no article
`kein` replaces `nicht` whenever the sentence contains `haben`
`nicht` is only used in questions, never in statements
`nicht` can only be used with verbs in the past tense

rubric: `kein` negates nouns that would have an indefinite article or none.
Distractors invent restrictions on `nicht` or `haben`.

items.prompt: Which of these verbs are separable verbs (the prefix splits off in a main clause)? Select all that apply.

options.label: einkaufen
aufstehen
anrufen
verstehen
bekommen

rubric: auf-, an- and ein- are separable prefixes.
ver- and be- are inseparable prefixes and never split off.

items.prompt: A learner reads `Ich habe gestern einen Film gesehen.` and asks why `gesehen` is at the end of the sentence. The learner knows this sentence talks about the past.

options.label: Past-tense sentences must end with the verb that carries the main meaning in the infinitive
In the perfect tense the auxiliary takes position two and the participle goes last
German always moves the last word of a sentence to the end for emphasis
The participle goes last because `Film` is a masculine accusative noun

rubric: In the perfect tense, `haben` or `sein` is the conjugated verb in second position and the participle closes the clause.
Distractors misattribute the position to emphasis, case or the infinitive.

items.prompt: Choose the correct article: `Ich gebe ___ Frau das Buch.`

options.label: den
der
die
dem

rubric: The recipient is dative, and dative feminine is `der`.
`die` is the nominative or accusative feminine form.

items.prompt: Choose the correct article: `Ich lege das Buch auf ___ Tisch.` (the book is being moved onto the table)

options.label: das
der
dem
den

rubric: Movement to a place with `auf` takes the accusative, and masculine accusative is `den`.
`dem` would describe a fixed location (dative).

items.prompt: What is the correct `du` form of `fahren` in the present tense?

options.label: fahren
fahrst
fährt
fährst

rubric: `fahren` has a vowel change a to ä in the du and er forms.
`fahrst` ignores the vowel change.

items.prompt: Which sentence has correct word order?

options.label: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil krank ich bin.
Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.
Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich bin krank.
Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil bin ich krank.

rubric: `weil` sends the conjugated verb to the end of its clause.
Other options keep main-clause order or scramble the words.

items.prompt: Which is the correct perfect tense of `Ich gehe nach Hause.`?

options.label: Ich habe nach Hause gegeht.
Ich bin nach Hause gegangen.
Ich bin nach Hause gegeht.
Ich habe nach Hause gegangen.

rubric: `gehen` is a verb of motion that uses `sein` with the participle `gegangen`.
Other options use `haben` or a regular participle form.

items.prompt: Which sentences use separable verbs correctly in a main clause? Select all that apply.

options.label: Er ruft mich morgen an.
Sie kauft im Supermarkt ein.
Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
Du anrufst mich oft.
Wir aufstehen früh.

rubric: The conjugated verb is in second position and the prefix goes to the end.
The other sentences keep the prefix attached to the conjugated verb.

items.prompt: You are texting a German friend about your weekend plans. You want to say: 'I want to visit my grandmother tomorrow.' You use `wollen` and `besuchen`, and `Oma` is the object. Which sentence is correct?

options.label: Morgen ich will meine Oma besuchen.
Ich besuchen will morgen meine Oma.
Ich will morgen meine Oma besuchen.
Ich will morgen besuchen meine Oma.

rubric: The modal verb is in second position and the infinitive goes to the end.
Distractors leave the infinitive in the middle or break verb-second order.

items.prompt: Choose the correct pair of articles: Der Hund liegt ___ Sofa, aber jetzt springt er ___ Sofa.

options.label: auf dem / auf dem
auf das / auf das
auf dem / auf das
auf das / auf dem

rubric: Location (wo?) takes dative and movement (wohin?) takes accusative with two-way prepositions.
Distractors swap or flatten the two cases.

items.prompt: Complete the sentence: Er sagt, dass er den Kuchen morgen ___.

options.label: mitbringen
bringt mit
mitbringt
mit bringt

rubric: Placeholder

items.prompt: Which German sentence correctly says 'Yesterday I had to work'?

options.label: Gestern musste ich arbeiten.
Gestern musste arbeiten ich.
Gestern musste ich gearbeitet.
Gestern ich musste arbeiten.

rubric: The finite verb stays in second position after the adverb and the subject follows; the infinitive goes last.
Distractors keep English order or misplace the infinitive or participle.

items.prompt: Complete the sentence: Er schenkt seiner Mutter einen ___ Ring.

options.label: teure
teures
teurer
teuren

rubric: After the indefinite article einen (masculine accusative) the adjective takes -en.
Distractors use endings from other genders or from unpreceded adjectives.

items.prompt: Complete the sentence: Das Haus ___ ist sehr groß.

options.label: mein Nachbar
meinem Nachbarn
meinen Nachbarn
meines Nachbarn

rubric: Possession is shown by the genitive: des/meines plus a weak masculine noun with -n.
Distractors use dative, nominative or accusative.

items.prompt: Which sentences have correct word order? Select all that apply.

options.label: Er fragt, ob sie heute Zeit hat.
Obwohl er krank war, er ging zur Arbeit.
Ich weiß, dass er morgen kommt.
Weil es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause.
Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich bin müde.

rubric: Subordinate clauses send the finite verb to the end, and a main clause after a subordinate clause starts with its verb.
Options 3 and 4 keep main-clause order inside weil or break inversion after obwohl.

items.prompt: You work in an office in Vienna. Your boss asks what you will do about a client who phoned while you were in a meeting. You want to say: 'I have to call the client back tomorrow.' Which sentence is correct?

options.label: Ich muss zurückrufen den Kunden morgen.
Ich muss den Kunden morgen zurückrufen.
Ich rufe muss den Kunden morgen zurück.
Ich muss den Kunden morgen rufen zurück.

rubric: With a modal verb the separable verb stays together as an infinitive at the end of the clause.
Distractors split the verb or misplace the modal or object.

items.prompt: Why is `ch` pronounced differently in `Buch` and `Bücher`?

options.label: The umlaut ü is a front vowel, so ch after it is the soft ich-sound [ç] instead of the back ach-sound [x].
The ü in Bücher is a long vowel, and ch after a long vowel takes the hard ach-sound, unlike after short vowels.
The plural ending -er shifts the stress onto the ending, and the weaker syllable before it softens ch into [ç].
The plural ending -er is a front-vowel suffix, so ch before it turns soft, whatever vowel stands before the ch.

rubric: The vowel before ch decides the sound: back vowels give [x], front vowels (including umlauts) give [ç].
Distractors blame the plural ending or vowel length rather than vowel position.

items.prompt: A learner says `Ich suche das Handytasche` for 'the phone case'. Which analysis explains the error?

options.label: In compounds the last noun sets the gender, so Tasche makes it die Handytasche, not das from Handy.
The article is right but the case is wrong: the accusative needs den before every compound noun.
Compounds take the gender of the first noun, so das is right, but a plural -n is missing.
Compounds are always neuter because they name a new thing, so das is right but the case is wrong.

rubric: The final component of a compound determines gender: die Tasche gives die Handytasche.
Distractors treat the first noun or neuter as default, or blame the case.

items.prompt: A learner writes: `Nachdem er das Buch gelesen hatte, er schrieb eine Kritik.` What is the error?

options.label: The subordinate clause fills position one, so the main clause verb must come next: schrieb er eine Kritik.
The comma should be removed so both clauses form one verb-final unit: ... hatte er eine Kritik schrieb.
Plusquamperfekt requires the main clause to use Plusquamperfekt too, so it should be hatte er geschrieben.
Nachdem is a coordinating conjunction, so the main clause keeps normal subject-verb order after the comma.

rubric: A subordinate clause at the start counts as the first element, so the main verb follows immediately and the subject comes after it.
Distractors invent tense agreement or misclassify nachdem.

items.prompt: A learner writes: `Er hat gestern nicht kommen gekonnt.` What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: Modal verbs cannot be used in the Perfekt, so Präteritum konnte is the only possible form.
kommen should be gekommen to match gekonnt: hat nicht gekommen gekonnt.
With another infinitive the modal appears as an infinitive, not a participle: hat nicht kommen können.
gekonnt is correct, but nicht must come after the participle: hat gestern kommen gekonnt nicht.

rubric: Perfekt with a modal plus another verb uses the double infinitive: hat kommen können.
Distractors deny Perfekt for modals or misplace participles and nicht.

items.prompt: In a casual chat message a learner writes: `Gestern ging ich ins Kino und sah einen Film.` Which diagnosis is best?

options.label: Gestern marks a completed action, so Perfekt is required here; Präteritum is ungrammatical with a past time adverb.
The grammar is fine, but chat about spoken events tends to use Perfekt; Präteritum reads as written.
The sentence is wrong because gehen and sehen are strong verbs, and strong verbs take Perfekt in most contexts.
Präteritum is mostly kept for sein, haben and modal verbs, so both verbs here are formed incorrectly.

rubric: Both tenses are grammatical; the choice reflects register, with Perfekt typical of informal spoken narration.
Distractors invent hard rules about strong verbs or time adverbs.

items.prompt: Which sentences contain a word-order error? Select all that apply.

options.label: Er hat gesagt, dass er kommt später.
Ich weiß nicht, warum er ist zu spät.
Im Sommer fahren wir nach Italien.
Heute Abend ich gehe ins Kino.

rubric: After a fronted element the verb stays second, and in subordinate clauses the finite verb goes last.
Option 2 is correct, so it is the only sentence without an error.

items.prompt: A learner writes three sentences: `Der Film fängt um acht an.` `Ich weiß, wann der Film an fängt.` `Kommst du mit?` The teacher marks only the second sentence. What is the error?

options.label: In a subordinate clause the prefix rejoins the verb at the end: wann der Film anfängt.
The word order should be verb-second even after wann: wann fängt der Film an.
The prefix should move before the subject: wann an der Film fängt.
The verb should become an infinitive with zu after wann: wann der Film anzufangen.

rubric: Separable prefixes only split when the finite verb is in second position; in verb-final clauses they join the verb.
Distractors apply main-clause order, misplace the prefix or add zu.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Obwohl er müde war, er arbeitete weiter." Which analysis correctly diagnoses the error?

options.label: Obwohl also sends the verb of the following main clause to the very end, so the sentence should read "er weiter arbeitete".
The comma after the subordinate clause resets the word order, so the subject can stay first in the main clause.
Obwohl is a coordinating conjunction, so the main clause keeps its normal subject-then-verb order after it.
The whole obwohl-clause fills position one, so the main-clause verb must follow at once: "arbeitete er weiter".

rubric: A fronted subordinate clause counts as the first element, so the finite verb comes next (inversion).
Distractors confuse obwohl with coordinating conjunctions or apply verb-final order to the main clause.

items.prompt: A learner asks about waiting for her brother and says "Worauf wartest du?", which a German speaker finds odd. Which analysis explains the problem?

options.label: The wo-form is right, but in a question it should move to the end of the clause, as in "Wartest du worauf?"
Warten auf takes the dative when the object is a person, so the question should be "Auf wem wartest du?"
Wo-compounds are normally used with separable verbs, and warten is inseparable, so it needs the plain preposition.
Wo-compounds ask about things or ideas; for a person you use preposition plus case: "Auf wen wartest du?"

rubric: Wo-/da-compounds replace preposition plus a thing; persons need preposition plus a case form of wer.
Distractors wrongly assign the dative to warten auf or invent separable-verb or word-position rules.

items.prompt: Compare "Wir sind im Garten gelaufen" with "Wir sind in den Garten gelaufen". Which analysis explains how the two differ?

options.label: Dative goes with sein-perfect verbs and accusative with haben-perfect verbs, so the case change reflects the auxiliary choice and not any difference in meaning.
The two sentences mean the same thing, and the accusative is only the more formal written variant that replaces the dative in careful, standard German.
Accusative shows that the garden is a definite, already-known garden, while dative shows that the garden is unspecified or mentioned for the first time.
Both use a two-way preposition with a motion verb, but dative places the running inside the garden and accusative makes the garden the goal.

rubric: With Wechselpräpositionen, dative marks location or the area of an activity; accusative marks direction toward a goal.
Distractors tie case to auxiliary choice, register or definiteness, which do not govern it.

items.prompt: A learner writes "Sie hat viele guten Freunde." Which analysis explains the mistake?

options.label: The ending should be -er, because Freunde is masculine and the phrase is the object, so "viele guter Freunde" is needed.
The adjective is declined as if viele were a definite article, but viele takes strong endings, so it is "viele gute Freunde".
The noun is wrong: after viele it must stand in the dative plural, so the sentence needs "vielen guten Freunden".
After quantity words like viele the adjective stays uninflected, as after etwas, so the form should be "viele gut Freunde".

rubric: Viele is not an article that carries the case ending, so the adjective takes the strong -e in nominative/accusative plural.
Distractors invent a case change, an uninflected adjective or a masculine -er ending.

items.prompt: A learner wants to say "because he had to come" in the perfect and writes "weil er kommen müssen hat". What is the correct form and why?

options.label: The learner's order is correct: in subordinate clauses all verb forms go to the end, with the auxiliary after the infinitives.
"weil hat er kommen müssen": the auxiliary moves to position two of the clause as in a main clause, then both infinitives follow.
"weil er kommen gemusst hat": modals always use the participle gemusst in subordinate clauses, so the auxiliary stays last.
"weil er hat kommen müssen": in a subordinate clause the auxiliary stands before a double infinitive, which replaces the participle.

rubric: With a modal plus infinitive in the perfect, the double infinitive appears and the finite auxiliary precedes it in verb-final clauses.
Distractors misuse the participle gemusst, keep the auxiliary last, or apply main-clause verb-second order.

items.prompt: In neutral word order (no special stress), which sentences place the objects correctly? Select all that apply.

options.label: Ich gebe das Buch ihm.
Ich gebe ihm das Buch.
Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch.
Ich gebe dem Mann es.
Ich gebe es dem Mann.

rubric: Neutral order puts a pronoun before a noun, and dative before accusative when both are nouns.
Options 1 and 3 put a pronoun after a noun object, which only works with special emphasis.

items.prompt: A learner writes "Ich freue mich auf das Geschenk" about a gift she received yesterday, and her tutor changes it to "über". Later she writes "Ich freue mich über die Ferien" about a holiday next month, and the tutor changes it to "auf". Which principle explains both corrections?

options.label: Auf marks formal written German and über marks everyday speech, so the tutor was adjusting the register of each sentence.
Über requires the accusative and auf requires the dative, so the changed articles forced the changes in preposition.
Auf looks forward to something still to come, while über expresses pleasure about something present or already received.
Auf goes with plural or abstract nouns, while über goes with singular concrete objects such as a gift.

rubric: Sich freuen auf looks ahead to a future event; sich freuen über reacts to a present or past one.
Distractors invent noun-type, case or register rules; both prepositions take the accusative here.

items.prompt: A teacher wants a rule for dass versus das that learners can apply reliably while writing. Criteria: it needs no grammar terms and rarely misfires. Which rule is best?

options.label: Write "dass" whenever a comma comes directly before the word, because only the conjunction can ever follow a comma in a sentence.
Try replacing the word with "dieses", "jenes" or "welches"; if one fits, write "das", otherwise write "dass".
Write "dass" whenever the sentence concerns a person's statement and "das" for objects, because meaning separates the two spellings.
Write "das" whenever a noun follows the word and "dass" whenever a verb follows it, because the next word shows the type.

rubric: The substitution test works for article, pronoun and relative uses of das without grammar terminology.
Distractors use surface cues (comma, next word, topic) that misfire often, e.g. relative clauses also follow commas.

items.prompt: A report must render the quote: Die Minister sagen: "Wir haben keine Zeit." as indirect speech. Criteria: formal register, same tense as the quote, and a verb form that differs from the indicative. Which sentence is best?

options.label: Die Minister sagen, sie hätten keine Zeit gehabt.
Die Minister sagen, sie hatten keine Zeit.
Die Minister sagen, sie hätten keine Zeit.
Die Minister sagen, sie haben keine Zeit.

rubric: Konjunktiv I "haben" equals the indicative in the plural, so Konjunktiv II "hätten" is used to mark reported speech.
Distractors keep the indicative, shift to the past, or change the tense to a past perfect meaning.

items.prompt: A learner keeps making article and adjective-ending errors across cases. Criterion: the study approach most likely to improve accuracy over the long term. Which is best?

options.label: Assign gender from natural sex, because this rule holds for nearly every noun, including words such as Mädchen and Weib.
Infer every gender from the noun ending alone, because the ending patterns cover all nouns and a list of exceptions is not needed.
Learn each noun with its article and plural, and use endings such as -ung or -chen only as a secondary check.
Learn nouns without articles at first, because the article can be attached later from the meaning of the word without much effort.

rubric: Articles drive case, adjective endings and pronouns, so gender must be stored with the noun; endings only help as a check.
Distractors rely on rules with many exceptions or postpone the article.

items.prompt: A learner's recording shows four habits. Criterion: rank by the risk of being misunderstood in conversation. Which habit carries the highest risk?

options.label: Voicing the final d in "Rad" instead of devoicing it, which sounds accented but leaves the word clear.
Using the ach-sound instead of the ich-sound in words like "ich", which is noticeable but rarely changes the word.
Pronouncing ö and ü as o and u, so "schön" and "schon" or "Bücher" and "Bucher" sound alike.
Using an English-style r instead of the uvular r, which sounds foreign but leaves nearly every word recognisable.

rubric: Rounded front vowels distinguish words, so merging them produces real misunderstandings.
The other habits mark an accent but seldom change the identity of a word.

items.prompt: A learner wants to sound natural telling a friend what happened yesterday. Criterion: natural in everyday speech, across most regions. Which guideline is best?

options.label: Use the Präteritum for every verb, since it is shorter and the Perfekt is kept for formal writing only.
Use the Perfekt for most verbs, but prefer the Präteritum for sein, haben and modals: "Ich war müde."
Use the Präteritum for regular verbs and the Perfekt for irregular verbs, since that split matches spoken usage.
Use the Perfekt for every verb, including sein and haben, so "Ich bin müde gewesen" is the natural choice.

rubric: Spoken narration favours the Perfekt, with Präteritum common for sein, haben and modals.
Distractors reverse the usage, over-apply the Perfekt, or invent a regular/irregular split.

items.prompt: A learner claims: "German word order is simply verb-second." Which criticisms of this claim are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: Non-finite verb parts such as participles and infinitives go to the clause end, splitting the verb.
Yes/no questions and imperatives put the finite verb in first position.
Subordinate clauses introduced by conjunctions like "weil" send the finite verb to the end.
Modal verbs are exempt from verb-second and always stand last in main clauses.
Verb-second fails whenever a time phrase opens the sentence, since the subject must then come first.

rubric: Verb-final subordinate clauses, verb-first questions and imperatives, and the sentence bracket all show the claim is oversimplified.
A fronted time phrase triggers inversion, which is consistent with verb-second; modals still stand in position two.

items.prompt: Priya has four weeks and 20 minutes a day before a trip to Austria. She wants to order food, ask directions and make small talk. Criteria: fastest usable speaking and listening, with errors that stay understandable. Which plan is best?

options.label: Memorise all four case tables with every article and adjective ending first, then start speaking in the fourth week of the plan.
Study the Konjunktiv I and genitive prepositions first, because polite service conversation relies on them more than on anything else.
Practise high-frequency chunks like "Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee" and "Wo ist der Bahnhof?" aloud, plus listening to slow dialogues.
Read graded newspaper articles silently every day, because heavy reading builds the grammar needed for fast spoken replies.

rubric: Spoken chunks with listening give immediate, usable phrases, and small case errors stay understandable.
Distractors delay speaking, prioritise rare forms, or train reading rather than the target skills.

items.prompt: A tutor claims: 'In German the finite verb is always the second element of the clause.' Which critique of this claim is most accurate?

options.label: Wrong because any adverb placed before the verb pushes it to third position in an ordinary declarative main clause
Correct as stated, because subordinate clauses also put the finite verb second, directly after the conjunction
Wrong because the verb is second only when the subject comes first and moves to the end once another element is fronted
Wrong for verb-final subordinate clauses and verb-first yes/no questions; it holds only for declarative main clauses

rubric: V2 describes declarative main clauses; subordinate clauses are verb-final and yes/no questions are verb-first.
Distractors target the belief that fronting a non-subject changes the verb's slot (it does not; the subject then follows the verb).

items.prompt: A learner wants to say 'I'm looking forward to the trip' (the trip is next month). Judged for grammatical accuracy and idiom, which version is best?

options.label: Ich freue mich auf die Reise, since auf marks anticipation of something still to come
Ich freue mich die Reise, since the reflexive verb already carries the meaning without a preposition
Ich freue mich über die Reise, since über is the standard preposition for any positive feeling
Ich freue mich für die Reise, since für marks the thing a feeling is directed toward

rubric: sich freuen auf + accusative expresses anticipation of a future event; über refers to present or past causes of joy.
Distractors reflect overgeneralising über or transferring English 'for'.

items.prompt: A formal written report must show unambiguously that the following is indirect speech: 'Die Kollegen haben keine Zeit.' Judged against that criterion, which version is best?

options.label: Sie sagten, die Kollegen habe keine Zeit, since Konjunktiv I is always required for reported speech
Sie sagten, die Kollegen haben keine Zeit, since the indicative is neutral and signals reported speech
Sie sagten, die Kollegen hätten keine Zeit, since Konjunktiv I would be identical to the indicative here
Sie sagten, die Kollegen hatten keine Zeit, since the Präteritum marks speech as reported

rubric: The plural Konjunktiv I 'haben' equals the indicative, so Konjunktiv II 'hätten' is used to mark the report clearly.
Distractors target using the indicative or Präteritum as markers, and applying singular 'habe' to a plural subject.

items.prompt: Which explanation best accounts for the adjective endings in 'ein alter Mann' versus 'der alte Mann' (both nominative)?

options.label: After der the adjective takes -e because it agrees with the article's definiteness, not with the noun's gender or case
Adjectives after any ein-word take -er, because ein marks the noun as indefinite and masculine in every case
The -er ending marks a plural, which appears whenever an indefinite article introduces a noun in the nominative
The adjective carries the gender-case signal (-er) where ein shows none; der already shows it, so -e suffices

rubric: Adjective endings supply the missing gender/case information: ein has no ending in masculine nominative, so the adjective takes -er.
Distractors misattribute the ending to definiteness, to ein-words in all cases, or to plural marking.

items.prompt: A tutor says: 'German noun gender is best predicted from meaning.' Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: Partly true for people and animals, but suffixes like -ung or -chen predict gender better; das Mädchen contradicts meaning
False, since gender is assigned randomly, so neither meaning nor endings help, and learners must memorise each noun with its article
Mostly true, since a suffix predicts gender only once the learner knows the meaning category, as with days, seasons and colours
True for inanimate nouns, since semantic groups like days, seasons and colours fix gender, and people nouns follow natural sex

rubric: Suffixes are often more reliable than meaning, and natural-sex mismatches like das Mädchen show meaning is not decisive.
Distractors overstate semantic rules or claim gender is entirely arbitrary.

items.prompt: Which are sound reasons to prefer würde + infinitive over the one-word Konjunktiv II in everyday speech? Select all that apply.

options.label: The one-word form is ungrammatical in subordinate clauses, so würde + infinitive is obligatory there
Sein, haben and modal verbs must use würde + infinitive, because they have no Konjunktiv II forms of their own
Some strong-verb forms, such as begänne or stünde, sound stilted or old-fashioned in conversation
For weak verbs the one-word form equals the Präteritum, so würde + infinitive keeps the hypothetical meaning clear

rubric: Ambiguity with the Präteritum and stilted strong forms are the real motivations.
Sein, haben and modals have common own forms (wäre, hätte, könnte), and subordinate clauses allow one-word forms.

items.prompt: You are proofreading an annual report. A colleague wrote 'Wegen dem schlechten Wetter wurde das Fest abgesagt.' The report is formal, must follow standard written grammar, and edits should be minimal. Which edit is best?

options.label: Leave it unchanged, since wegen takes the dative and the genitive is only used in poetry
Change to 'Wegen des schlechten Wetters', since formal written German standardly takes the genitive after wegen
Change to 'Aufgrund dem schlechten Wetter', since aufgrund is always formal and takes the dative
Change to 'Wegen das schlechte Wetter', since wegen takes the accusative like other causal prepositions

rubric: Standard written German uses the genitive after wegen; the dative is common in speech.
Distractors confuse spoken usage with the written norm or assign the wrong case.

items.prompt: Build one sentence that begins with a wenn-clause, expresses an unreal past condition, and has correct word order in the main clause. Which sentence does it?

options.label: Wenn ich das gewusst hätte, ich wäre nicht gekommen
Wenn ich das wüsste, wäre ich nicht gekommen
Wenn ich das gewusst hätte, wäre ich nicht gekommen
Wenn ich hätte gewusst das, wäre ich nicht gekommen

rubric: Past unreal condition needs Konjunktiv II past (hätte gewusst / wäre gekommen), and the main clause after a fronted subordinate clause starts with the verb.
Distractors miss inversion, use present Konjunktiv II, or break verb-final order.

items.prompt: Rewrite 'der Vertrag, der gestern unterschrieben wurde' as a compact attribute before the noun, keeping the passive meaning and using the correct ending after der. Which does it?

options.label: der gestern unterschrieben Vertrag
der gestern unterschriebener Vertrag
der gestern unterschriebene Vertrag
der gestern unterschreibende Vertrag

rubric: The past participle with an adjective ending (-e after der) conveys a completed passive action.
Distractors use the active present participle, omit the ending, or use the strong ending after der.

items.prompt: You design a drill for English speakers on the ich-Laut/ach-Laut, whose choice depends on the preceding vowel. Which drill best makes that rule audible while keeping the stem constant?

options.label: Stem pairs that change vowel, like Buch–Bücher and Tuch–Tücher, so the sound shift follows the vowel
Pairs such as Dach–Dack, so learners hear the contrast between fricative and stop and learn which spelling gives each sound
Repeated isolated ich and ach words, since each word has its own fixed sound that cannot be predicted from neighbours
Minimal pairs such as mich–misch, so learners separate the ch sound from the sch sound across identical vowels

rubric: Stem alternations like Buch–Bücher show the back-vowel/front-vowel conditioning of [x] and [ç].
Distractors drill a different contrast or treat the sounds as unpredictable.

items.prompt: Form a single compound for 'front-door key' that names the key (not the door), and give it with its correct article.

options.label: der Haustürschlüssel, since the last noun is the head and fixes gender
das Türhausschlüssel, since compounds with several nouns default to neuter
die Schlüsselhaustür, since the first noun, Schlüssel, names the object and fixes gender
die Haustürschlüssel, since the noun nearest the article, Tür, fixes gender

rubric: The last element is the head of a German compound and determines both meaning and gender: der Schlüssel.
Distractors misplace the head or invent a neuter default.

items.prompt: Translate 'I would gladly have come, but I had to work' so that the first clause uses Konjunktiv II past with the correct auxiliary for kommen, and the second uses the Präteritum. Which does it?

options.label: Ich wäre gern gekommen, aber ich müsste arbeiten
Ich würde gern kommen, aber ich habe arbeiten müssen
Ich hätte gern gekommen, aber ich musste arbeiten
Ich wäre gern gekommen, aber ich musste arbeiten

rubric: Kommen takes sein, so Konjunktiv II past is 'wäre gekommen'; 'musste' is Präteritum.
Distractors use haben, an ungrammatical würde + participle, or Konjunktiv II in the second clause.

items.prompt: A proposed case cheat sheet lists only the article tables for nominative, accusative, dative and genitive. Which additions would fix its main gaps? Select all that apply.

options.label: Adjective endings that change depending on the determiner before them
A rule that all feminine nouns add -n in the dative singular
A list of prepositions that govern the nominative
Weak masculine nouns such as der Student take -en in every case except the nominative singular

rubric: Weak (n-declension) nouns and determiner-dependent adjective endings are real case phenomena missing from article tables.
Feminine nouns take no dative singular -n, and no prepositions govern the nominative.

items.prompt: A learner writes 'Ich anrufe dich morgen' and 'Ich habe dich anrufen.' You design a mini-lesson that must show where the prefix goes in a main clause, in a verb-final subordinate clause, and in the Perfekt. Which example set meets all three requirements?

options.label: Ich rufe dich morgen an. / Ich weiß, dass ich dich morgen anrufe. / Ich habe dich gestern angerufen.
Ich rufe dich morgen an. / Rufst du mich an? / Ich habe dich gestern angerufen.
Ich rufe dich morgen an. / Ich weiß, dass ich dich morgen anrufe. / Ich will dich morgen anrufen.
Ich weiß, dass ich dich morgen anrufe. / Ich habe dich gestern angerufen. / Ich will dich morgen anrufen.

rubric: Only the last set shows the split prefix in a main clause, the joined verb in a subordinate clause, and ge- inside the participle.
Other sets omit the subordinate clause, the split main-clause form, or the Perfekt.
